challenges.name: rendering-models-quiz
challenges.title: Why did the catalog go dynamic?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the catalog incident: the layout and build output before the fix, and the response header after it.

questions.explanation: False. The build output marks /courses as ƒ, rendered on demand: a route is rendered for each request as soon as anything in its tree (the page or any layout above it) reads a request-time API such as cookies(), headers() or searchParams. The root layout reads cookies() for the theme, so every route below it, the catalog included, is rendered per request and revalidate = 300 cannot cache the HTML (depending on your Next.js version it may still affect how the data fetches inside are cached, but not the page). The misconception is that revalidate is a setting of the page alone; the whole tree decides, and one cookie read in a shared layout outranks it. The fix is to stop reading the cookie on the server, then confirm in the build output that the route is no longer ƒ.

True. x-nextjs-cache: HIT means this response was served from the Next.js cache, which is one copy of the HTML for everyone; nothing in it can depend on who asked. A per-visitor detail like the theme therefore moves to the browser: the inline script reads the cookie and sets data-theme before the page is painted, which avoids a flash of the wrong theme. suppressHydrationWarning on <html> is needed because the script changes that attribute before React hydrates. The misconception is that you can keep a cached page and still personalise its HTML on the server; you can personalise it in the browser, or render that part per request, but not both cache and vary the same HTML.

challenges.name: choose-rendering-strategy
challenges.title: Choose a rendering strategy for every route
challenges.description: After the catalog incident (GET /courses was rendered on every request because the root layout read cookies() for the theme, and TTFB tripled under load), the CodeDev team runs the traits of every route through one function before each release. Write chooseRendering(page), which returns { route, strategy, reason } for a page { route, freshnessSeconds, perUserData, reads, pageCount, dataAtBuild, seo }. freshnessSeconds is how old the HTML may be (null = it changes only with a deploy, 0 = it must be fresh on every request); reads lists the request-time APIs read by the page or any layout above it; pageCount is how many pages the route produces; dataAtBuild says whether the data source can be reached during next build. Apply the rules in this order: (1) invalid traits give strategy "invalid" and reason "invalid traits": freshnessSeconds that is not null and not a whole number >= 0, pageCount that is not a whole number >= 1, or reads that is not an array or contains anything other than "cookies", "headers", "searchParams". (2) perUserData true: "dynamic", reason "per-user data". (3) reads not empty: "dynamic", reason "reads " followed by the distinct names it contains in the fixed order cookies, headers, searchParams, joined with ", " (for example "reads cookies, searchParams"). (4) freshnessSeconds 0: "dynamic", reason "must be fresh on every request". (5) The HTML is "prerendered at build" when dataAtBuild is true and pageCount is at most 1000, otherwise it is "rendered on first request". (6) freshnessSeconds null: "static", reason = the text from rule 5. (7) freshnessSeconds above 0: strategy "isr:<seconds>" (for example "isr:300"), reason = the text from rule 5 + ", revalidated every <seconds> s". seo never changes the strategy: static, ISR and dynamic pages all send complete HTML to crawlers. The test runner reads a list of pages as JSON and prints one decision per page.
hints: Which traits make the HTML depend on the request itself, and should they be checked before or after the freshness window? A page cannot be cached for 5 minutes if its HTML depends on who is asking.

Follow the rule order in the starter comment: validity, perUserData, reads, then freshnessSeconds. Filtering the fixed list ["cookies", "headers", "searchParams"] by what the page reads gives the names in the right order with no duplicates. Watch out: 0 and null are both falsy in JavaScript, but here they mean opposite things.

A trace on a route that is not in the tests: /instructors/[id] with freshnessSeconds 600, pageCount 2000, dataAtBuild true, reads [] and perUserData false passes rules 1 to 4; 2000 is above the build limit, so the HTML is rendered on first request, and the strategy is isr:600 with the reason "rendered on first request, revalidated every 600 s". With reads ["headers", "cookies", "headers"] it stops at rule 3: dynamic, "reads cookies, headers".
